strengths: Identifies and rigorously formalizes a genuine scalability gap: existing IIEFG solvers (CFR+, MMD, etc.) scale with action-space size, while continuous-action solvers (JPSPG) are restricted to pseudoconcave/monotone game classes; this paper targets differential games under Isaacs' condition where neither limitation need apply.

The core theoretical contribution (Thm. 4.1) is elegant and well-motivated: it connects the classical 'Cav u' theorem from repeated incomplete-information games (Aumann et al., De Meyer, Cardaliaguet) to a primal-dual DP/backward-induction formulation for differential games, showing equilibrium strategies are at most I- and (I+1)-atomic. This yields a genuinely useful reformulation (splitting into P1/P2 subproblems) that removes dependence on action-space discretization.

Provides careful supporting theory: convergence of the discretized DPs to the continuous game value (Thm 3.1, building on Cardaliaguet 2009), an explicit error-propagation/complexity analysis for the naive backward-induction baseline (Thm 4.2), and multiple pedagogical analytical examples (repeated games, beer-quiche, Hexner's game) worked out in the appendix that build strong intuition and partially verify the framework by hand.

The multigrid (FAS) extension to accelerate backward induction over many time steps is a novel and practically useful addition, giving substantial wall-clock speedups (roughly 2.5-3x) in the reported experiments.

Empirical comparisons against multiple relevant baselines (CFR+, MMD, DeepCFR, JPSPG, CFR-BR-Primal) are reasonably thorough for the chosen benchmark, showing the proposed method (CAMS) is invariant to action-space discretization size while baselines scale poorly, and yields strategies closer to the known analytical Nash equilibrium.
Demonstrates some scalability beyond the base case, including a 10-stage state-constrained game and a higher-dimensional (3D, 6D joint action) Hexner variant.
weaknesses: The problem class is fairly restrictive (zero-sum, Isaacs' condition/pure-NE requirement, one-sided information where the informed player knows everything about the other), and all empirical validation is confined to a single family of linear-quadratic differential games (Hexner's game) with known analytical solutions; no nonlinear-dynamics or more realistic attack-defense scenario (despite motivating examples like missile defense/football in the intro) is tested.

The paper's own complexity analysis is with respect to the number of types I, but there is no empirical or theoretical study of how the method scales as I grows beyond 2; the stated regime of applicability (I^2 << |U|+|V|) is asserted but not stress-tested.

Multigrid results (Table 2) report only wall-clock runtime improvements, without any evaluation of how the restriction/prolongation approximation affects final value or strategy accuracy relative to the non-multigrid baseline or ground truth—an important omission given multigrid introduces additional approximation error.

Theorem 4.2 shows the baseline algorithm has complexity exponential in the number of time steps K; while multigrid is proposed as a fix, there is no theoretical guarantee (only empirical evidence on 3 settings) that multigrid actually breaks this exponential dependence, so the scalability claim over time steps rests mainly on limited empirical evidence.

The value networks rely on input-convex neural network architectures to encode convexity in belief, which is a strong structural assumption; its effect on approximation quality/capacity is not empirically ablated.

Some baseline comparisons may be somewhat foregone conclusions, since CFR+/MMD/DeepCFR are not designed for continuous state/action/time differential games and are expected to scale poorly with discretization; a more informative comparison might include stronger continuous-action or PDE-based differential-game baselines beyond JPSPG.

The manuscript is dense and notation-heavy, pushing most of the technical substance (proofs, additional worked examples, full algorithms) into a very long appendix, which may hurt accessibility and self-containedness of the main text.

Reported error/runtime metrics for the main experiments (e.g., action error, tr estimates) are based on relatively few trajectories (50-100) without variance/confidence analysis beyond simple standard deviations, limiting statistical confidence in comparative claims.

strengths: The paper builds on a solid theoretical foundation (Aumann et al.'s Cav u theorem, Cardaliaguet's differential game with asymmetric information theory, De Meyer's dual game) and makes a genuinely useful connection between this classical theory and the modern IIEFG solver literature, which appears to be a real gap.

Theorem 4.1 (the atomic/splitting structure of equilibrium strategies under Isaacs' condition) is an elegant and non-trivial insight that explains why continuous action spaces do not need to be discretized for this class of games, and is rigorously proven in the appendix.

The paper is unusually thorough in providing proofs, worked analytical examples (Hexner's game, a zero-sum beer-quiche turn-based game), and a detailed complexity analysis (Theorem 4.2) including comparison to existing CFR/FTRL/MMD complexity bounds.

Empirical comparisons include a reasonably wide set of relevant baselines (CFR+, MMD, DeepCFR, JPSPG, CFR-BR-Primal) and clearly show that CAMS's cost is invariant to action-space discretization while baselines scale poorly.

The multigrid extension for reducing cost over many time steps is a practically useful engineering contribution with clear empirical runtime gains (roughly 2-3x speedup reported across 4/10/16-stage games).
Validation against an analytically solvable game (Hexner's) with known ground-truth critical time and equilibrium trajectories lends credibility to the correctness of the solver.
weaknesses: The problem class is quite narrow: requires Isaacs' condition, control-affine dynamics, strictly zero-sum payoffs, and one-sided information — this restricts applicability substantially relative to the general framing and title's claim of a 'scalable solver' for differential games.

All empirical evaluation is conducted on variants of essentially a single game family (Hexner's game, including a 3D extension) — there is no demonstration on qualitatively different game structures, raising concerns about generalization of the reported gains.

Theorem 4.2 shows the baseline algorithm's complexity is exponential in the number of time steps (C^{2K}); multigrid only empirically mitigates this without a theoretical convergence/complexity guarantee, so the core scalability claim in the title is only partially substantiated.

Some baseline comparisons appear to be run under constrained budgets or modified forms (e.g., 'CFR-BR-Primal' is a custom simplification, DeepCFR/JPSPG given limited iterations/traversals), which makes it harder to assess whether comparisons are fully fair versus tuned baselines.

Key theoretical results (e.g., Theorem 3.1, much of the DP formulation) are largely restatements/completions of proofs from prior work (Cardaliaguet 2009, Aumann et al. 1995, De Meyer 1996), somewhat limiting the incremental theoretical novelty beyond the splitting/atomic-strategy insight and its algorithmic exploitation.

The paper notes P2's (uninformed player's) strategy approximation has visibly higher error than P1's without deeper investigation or mitigation, which is concerning since P2's robust strategy is central to the stated attack-defense motivation.
No error bars, confidence intervals, or repeated-run statistics are reported for most of the reported metrics (Fig. 3, Table 2), limiting confidence in the significance of reported improvements.

Scalability to higher-dimensional state/action spaces beyond the 3D Hexner extension is not explored, leaving open questions about how value-network training and minimax solving scale with state dimensionality in practice.

strengths: Novel and non-trivial theoretical insight connecting the classical 'Cav u' theorem for incomplete-information games to the structure of equilibria in continuous-action differential games, showing that under Isaacs' condition the informed/uninformed players' strategies are I- and (I+1)-atomic respectively, decoupling computational complexity from action-space size.

Clean primal-dual DP (splitting) reformulation that reduces solving the continuous-action minimax to finite-dimensional mixed-integer-like problems, with a rigorous proof sketch and detailed appendix derivation (Thm 4.1, App. B).

The multigrid (FAS) extension to backward induction for nonlinear HJI-type value approximation is a creative and reasonably well worked-out engineering contribution, with clear empirical speedups (roughly 2-3x) across 4/10/16-stage games.

Strong grounding in established differential game theory (Cardaliaguet, Aumann et al., De Meyer) with detailed connections explained via toy examples (repeated games, beer-quiche game, Hexner's game) in the appendix, aiding reproducibility and understanding.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical comparison against multiple relevant baselines (CFR+, MMD, CFR-BR, DeepCFR, JPSPG) showing CAMS's cost is invariant to action discretization while baselines scale poorly.
Demonstrates some scalability beyond the toy setting via a 3D (12D state, 6D action) Hexner's game variant and a state-constrained variant with safe-set restriction.
weaknesses: Empirical validation is essentially confined to a single family of games (linear-quadratic Hexner's game and its constrained/3D variants), which admits closed-form solutions; it remains unclear how the method performs on nonlinear dynamics or more complex payoff structures where Isaacs' condition and pure best responses are harder to verify or compute.

The claimed 'scalability' is undercut by the paper's own Theorem 4.2, which shows the baseline algorithm's complexity is exponential in the number of time steps K (and grows with I^2); multigrid provides only constant-factor empirical speedups (2-3x) rather than addressing this exponential scaling fundamentally.

Experiments use a small number of game types (I=2) throughout; since much of the paper's complexity analysis hinges on I, no experiments probe how performance/accuracy degrades as I grows, leaving the core scalability claim in the abstract only partially substantiated.

Baseline comparisons may not be entirely apples-to-apples: DeepCFR is run for a limited number of iterations/traversals and CAMS uses a much tighter convergence threshold (1e-5 vs 1e-3 for baselines), which could bias comparisons; wall-clock numbers in Table 2 and the 4-stage comparison lack variance/multiple-seed reporting.

The approach relies on several strong assumptions (Isaacs' condition, control-affine/compact action-state sets, full mutual knowledge of dynamics/payoffs except type, perfect recall) that considerably narrow applicability relative to general IIEFGs, and this restriction is not always made salient in the framing of contributions.

The paper is extremely dense with most technical content (proofs, additional examples, algorithmic details) relegated to a very long appendix (32 pages), making the main 8-page submission hard to fully assess/verify on its own and raising reproducibility concerns for readers who do not engage with the appendix.

No direct empirical comparison to the closest related prior work (Ghimire et al., 2024) on the state-constrained differential game setting, despite building directly on its safe-set technique; only a qualitative complexity comparison is given.

strengths: Genuine theoretical contribution: the paper proves that equilibrium behavioral strategies in a well-motivated subclass of 2p0s differential games with one-sided information (2p0s1) are atomic (I-atomic for P1, (I+1)-atomic for P2), extending classical results from repeated games (Aumann et al. 1995; De Meyer 1996) to the differential-game setting building on Cardaliaguet (2007) and Ghimire et al. (2024). The primal-dual reformulation and consistency/error propagation analysis (Thm 4.2, Thm 5.1) are technically careful, with detailed appendix proofs.

Demonstrates the practical utility of the theory across three distinct solution paradigms (value approximation with a novel multigrid FAS extension, model-free MARL with PPO/MMD, and differentiable MPC), showing the structural insight is broadly actionable rather than a purely theoretical curiosity.

Strong empirical validation on Hexner's game, which has an analytical closed-form NE, allowing precise measurement of solution accuracy against several competitive SOTA baselines (CFR+, MMD, CFR-BR, DeepCFR, JPSPG, PPO, R-NaD), with consistent, sizable improvements in both accuracy and computational cost, and U-invariance of the proposed method versus baselines that scale poorly with discretized action size.

An ambitious and compelling large-scale demonstration: a 22-player, continuous-action American football game (K=10, U=∞) solved in ~30 minutes on a laptop, with emergent behavior (information concealment for ~0.5s) plausibly matching real-world coaching intuition, illustrating real-world relevance to sports, defense, and other one-sided-information domains.

Reasonably thorough reproducibility effort: detailed appendices with algorithm pseudocode (multigrid), hyperparameters, derivations for Hexner's game and a beer-quiche-like turn-based example, and football-game dynamics specification.
weaknesses: The theoretical results depend on fairly restrictive assumptions (deterministic dynamics, Isaacs' condition, small discrete I, full model knowledge/observability), and the paper explicitly notes that stochastic dynamics/observations break the precise belief control needed for the atomic structure, leaving a major generalization direction unaddressed.

Novelty is somewhat incremental relative to very recent prior work by the same/overlapping research thread (Ghimire et al., 2024, ICML) and classical repeated-game results (Aumann et al., De Meyer); the core structural insight (atomic NE via convexification) is not new in spirit, and this paper's contribution is mainly the extension to differential games plus algorithmic integration.

The headline football demonstration is a single, largely qualitative case study (compared informally to a coaching blog's ~1-second estimate) without statistical replication, sensitivity analysis, or quantitative ground truth, making it more illustrative than rigorously validated; the simulated dynamics (soft/differentiable tackling, 2D point-mass players) are a significant simplification of real football.

The claimed complexity reduction to I^K (or (I+1)^K) still scales exponentially in K, so scalability to longer horizons remains a concern; multigrid helps constant factors but the asymptotic exponential dependence on K (per Thm 5.1, complexity ~C^{2K}) is not eliminated.

Empirical validation of the atomic-structure benefit is essentially limited to I=2 throughout (Hexner's game and football); there is no exploration of how performance/scalability changes as I grows, which is central to the paper's stated advantage over generic IIEFG solvers (I ≪ U).

The paper is dense and notation-heavy, with many key derivations deferred entirely to the appendix; this may hinder accessibility and independent verification without significant effort, and some claims (e.g., DS-GDA's guarantees only being sublinear for nonconvex-nonconcave problems) imply the practical NE achieved is only approximate, which is not fully reconciled with the strong accuracy claims in experiments.

strengths: Provides a rigorous theoretical extension of the atomic equilibrium-structure results (previously known for repeated games with one-sided incomplete information, e.g., Aumann et al., De Meyer) to differential games, with detailed proofs (Thms 4.1, 4.2, 5.1) connecting primal/dual game reformulations, viscosity-solution theory, and convexification arguments.

The reduction of game-tree complexity from U^{2K} to I^K/(I+1)^K is a meaningful theoretical insight when I << U, and is clearly motivated and explained (e.g., via Fig. 2's convexification illustration).

Reasonably comprehensive empirical comparison against many established solvers (CFR+, MMD, CFR-BR, JPSPG, DeepCFR, PPO, R-NaD) across normal-form and multi-stage settings, with both computational cost and solution-accuracy metrics reported.
The multigrid extension to accelerate value approximation for the nonlinear Hamilton-Jacobi PDEs is a nice practical addition with demonstrated wall-clock savings (Table 1).

The 22-player football demonstration is an ambitious and interesting proof-of-concept showing the framework can be applied to a large-scale, continuous-action, multi-agent setting that would be intractable for standard IIEFG solvers.
Analytical validation via Hexner's game and a zero-sum beer-quiche game provides sanity checks that the proposed primal-dual machinery recovers known closed-form equilibria.
weaknesses: The core theoretical result (atomic NE structure) is an extension/adaptation of prior results (Aumann et al. 1995, De Meyer 1996, Cardaliaguet 2007, Ghimire et al. 2024) rather than a fundamentally new phenomenon; the novelty is incremental (differential-game extension) despite being described with strong claims.

The framework relies on several restrictive assumptions (deterministic dynamics, Isaacs' condition, full state/action observability, one-sided information only) that are explicitly acknowledged as failing to generalize to stochastic dynamics/observations, substantially narrowing real-world applicability (footnote in Remarks admits belief cannot be precisely controlled otherwise).

Despite the claimed complexity collapse, the remaining I^K (or (I+1)^K) complexity is still exponential in K; for anything beyond small I and moderate K (e.g., the reported case with I=2), scalability benefits are limited, and the paper doesn't clearly characterize where the method breaks down as I or K grow.

The football demonstration, while visually compelling, rests on a highly stylized soft-contact/double-integrator abstraction of football, and the validation against real-world tactics is anecdotal (a single blog citation about a '~1 second' concealment window versus the model's 0.5s), which is weak empirical support for the claimed practical significance.

Baseline comparisons may not be entirely fair: DeepCFR and JPSPG are given limited iterations/traversals with wall-clock budgets set relative to CAMS, and hyperparameter tuning effort across methods is not clearly matched or justified, raising concerns about baseline competitiveness.

Several empirical results (e.g., R-NaD outperforming MMD/PPO, contradicting prior work) are noted anecdotally without deeper investigation or ablation to explain the discrepancy, weakening confidence in the robustness of the MARL comparisons.

The paper packs together many contributions (theory, multigrid PDE solver, MARL adaptation, MPC, football case study), which, combined with dense notation and proofs deferred to a long appendix, reduces clarity and makes it hard to assess the depth/rigor of any single component within the space provided.

No statistical uncertainty (e.g., variance across seeds/random initial states) is reported for most of the key comparison plots (Figs. 3, 5), limiting confidence in the significance of the reported improvements.

The claimed 'solving football' framing somewhat overstates the contribution given the simplified game abstraction (no realistic player behavior models beyond kinematics, no interaction with actual play data, small K=10).

strengths: Strong theoretical contribution: proves that Nash equilibrium strategies in 2p0s1 differential games are I-atomic for the informed player and (I+1)-atomic for the uninformed player, extending known results from repeated games (Aumann et al., De Meyer) to the differential game setting with rigorous proofs (Thm 4.1, 4.2) and detailed appendix derivations.
The primal-dual reformulation (Gτ and G*τ) is elegant and well-justified, with a clear connection to convex/concave envelope theory (Cav u theorem) and a clean geometric intuition (Fig. 2).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three learning paradigms (value approximation, model-free MARL, MPC) against a wide range of strong baselines (CFR+, MMD, CFR-BR, JPSPG, DeepCFR, PPO, R-NaD), demonstrating consistent and often dramatic improvements in both accuracy and computational cost.
The multigrid scheme for accelerating value approximation is a nice practical contribution that meaningfully reduces wall-clock time (e.g., ~2.5-3x speedup in Table 1).

The 22-player American football demonstration is an impressive and compelling real-world-scale application showing the practical value of the theory, with results that qualitatively match known coaching literature on play-concealment timing.

Theorem 4.2 with detailed proof (via consistency/semiconcavity arguments) rigorously establishes convergence of the discretized primal-dual scheme to the true differential game value as τ→0, going beyond prior sketches (e.g., Cardaliaguet 2009).
Analytical validation on Hexner's game and a zero-sum beer-quiche variant provides good sanity checks with closed-form ground truth.
weaknesses: The theory relies on fairly restrictive assumptions (A1-A5): deterministic dynamics, Isaacs' condition, one-sided information only, and compact/Lipschitz structure. The authors acknowledge that stochastic dynamics/observations break the precise belief control needed for the atomic structure, which limits applicability to some of the claimed application domains (e.g., missile defense, cybersecurity, which often involve stochastic elements).

The scalability advantage is contingent on I being small (I≪U); the football demo only uses I=2. It remains unclear how the approach scales as I grows, since the reformulated minimax problems and game-tree complexity still grow as I^K (or (I+1)^K), which could become intractable for even modest I with large K.

Validation of the football result is largely qualitative (comparing 0.5s concealment time to a reported ~1.0s coaching estimate from a blog source), which is a weak form of ground-truth validation for the central real-world demonstration.

Reproducibility is a concern: many implementation details (multigrid pseudocode, network architectures, hyperparameters) are relegated to a lengthy appendix, and it's unclear if code/data will be released; some experimental setups (e.g., R-NaD with 'little to no hyperparameter tuning') suggest baseline comparisons may not be fully optimized.
The paper's writing is dense with heavy notational overhead, which may hinder accessibility and broader impact despite the technical strength.

The claimed complexity reduction (I^K vs U^2K) is somewhat idealized since it assumes P2 plays pure best responses (primal) or P1 plays pure best responses (dual) rather than solving the full simultaneous NE, and computing the true joint equilibrium still requires combining both primal and dual solves plus per-node nonconvex-nonconcave minimax optimization (DS-GDA), whose own convergence guarantees are only sublinear.
